hook.line: Some things get under your skin before you can name them: a message left on read, a wait that drags on. Spanish puts the cause first and you are the one it lands on.
hook.es: Me pone nerviosa que no contestes los mensajes.
hook.en: It makes me nervous when you don't answer my messages. (a woman speaking, to a friend)

examples.es: Me pone nerviosa que no contestes los mensajes.
examples.en: It makes me nervous when you don't answer my messages. (a woman speaking, to a friend)

examples.es: Me desespera la lentitud de este trámite.
examples.en: The slowness of this process drives me crazy.
In the end I lost my patience.

examples.es: Me pone muy nervioso que Vale no diga nada.
examples.en: It makes me very nervous that Vale says nothing. (a man speaking)
The wait makes me nervous. (a woman speaking)

examples.es: No me pone nervioso hablar en público.
examples.en: Speaking in public doesn't make me nervous. (a man speaking)

rule:
The cause is the subject, and you are the *me* it lands on: *me pone nervioso* is "it makes me nervous".

Say *nervioso* or *nerviosa* for who is speaking. Add *muy* to turn it up.

After it comes a noun (*la espera*), an infinitive (*hablar en público*) or *que* plus the wish form (*que no contestes*).

*Me desespera* is stronger: it drives me crazy. For the breaking point, *perder la paciencia*: *perdí la paciencia*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *poner* plus an adjective a verb of change: it says what state something puts you in.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right form and type the whole sentence (a woman speaking): *Me pone ___ que no contestes.* (*nerviosa* or *nervioso*)
yourTurn.answer: Me pone nerviosa que no contestes.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (a man speaking): It makes me nervous that Vale says nothing.
yourTurn.answer: Me pone nervioso que Vale no diga nada.
yourTurn.why: The cause is the subject, then *que* and the wish form: *diga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The slowness of this process drives me crazy.
yourTurn.answer: Me desespera la lentitud de este trámite.
yourTurn.why: *Me desespera* is followed directly by the thing that does it.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: In the end I lost my patience.
yourTurn.why: It happened once, so *perdí*, with *la paciencia*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It makes me nervous that they're always late. (a woman speaking)
yourTurn.answer: Me pone nerviosa que siempre lleguen tarde.
accept: Me pone nerviosa que lleguen siempre tarde.
yourTurn.why: The late ones are *they*, so the wish form is *lleguen*.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it up: *Me pone nervioso que Vale no diga nada.* Say "very".
yourTurn.answer: Me pone muy nervioso que Vale no diga nada.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Me pone nervioso hablar en público.*
yourTurn.answer: No me pone nervioso hablar en público.

pitfalls.wrong: Me pone nerviosa que no contestas los mensajes.
pitfalls.right: Me pone nerviosa que no contestes los mensajes.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After a feeling plus *que*, the verb takes the wish form: *contestes*.

pitfalls.wrong: Yo desespero la lentitud de este trámite.
pitfalls.right: Me desespera la lentitud de este trámite.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The slowness is what does the driving crazy, and you are the *me*.
Almost. Spanish says *la paciencia* here, not *mi paciencia*.

personal: Say one thing that makes you nervous, or drives you crazy. Start with *Me pone nervioso…*, *Me pone nerviosa…* or *Me desespera…*
